common_name: Golden Marinka Fuchsia (Variegated Gold-Leaf Trailing Red Fuchsia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants after frost danger has passed in rich, well-drained, evenly moist potting mix in shade to partial shade; a golden-variegated sport of the classic Marinka fuchsia, grown as much for its foliage as its flowers.

directions: Grow in a hanging basket or shaded container filled with rich, well-drained, evenly moist potting mix. Golden Marinka is a sport of the century-old trailing cultivar Marinka, bearing the same single deep red flowers on a vigorous cascading plant, but with leaves broadly margined in creamy gold that brighten through the season and give the basket color even between flushes of bloom. The variegated foliage colors most vividly in bright, indirect light but can scorch in hot direct sun, so afternoon shade is important. It has little cold tolerance and dries out quickly as a basket plant, so in the Gulf South site it in a shaded, breezy spot with frequent watering and bring it under cover well before the first fall frost.

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; a white-flowered hardy fuchsia discovered in the Lake District village of Hawkshead and carrying the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Hawkshead bears small, narrow, near-white flowers tinged faintly green at the tube, a departure from the red-and-purple coloring typical of hardy fuchsias, on a dense, upright, twiggy bush that flowers from early summer through fall. Its fine-textured foliage and abundant pale blooms make it a useful contrast plant among more brightly colored hardy fuchsias and companion perennials, and it draws hummingbirds despite its subdued color. It dies back to the ground in colder winters and resprouts from the roots each spring. In the humid, hot summers of the Gulf South it performs best with afternoon shade and consistent soil moisture, and a heavy winter mulch over the crown improves its odds of returning at the cooler edge of its hardiness range.

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; a variegated sport found at the National Trust garden of Sharpitor in Devon and holder of the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Sharpitor bears soft gray-green leaves broadly edged in creamy white, setting off pale pink-and-lilac flowers that are noticeably softer in color than the red-and-purple blooms typical of hardy fuchsias, and it flowers from summer into fall. Its variegated foliage stays attractive from spring through frost even when the plant is not in bloom, making it as much a foliage accent as a flowering shrub in a mixed border. It dies back in cold winters and resprouts from the roots in spring, but is slightly less cold-hardy than green-leaved Fuchsia magellanica forms. In the humid, hot summers of the Gulf South, give it afternoon shade and consistent moisture, since the pale variegated leaves can scorch in strong sun, and mulch heavily over winter to protect the crown.

common_name: Lady Thumb Fuchsia (Dwarf Pink-and-White Hardy Fuchsia)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; a dwarf sport of Tom Thumb with semi-double pink-and-white flowers, holder of the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Lady Thumb arose as a sport of the dwarf hardy fuchsia Tom Thumb and shares its compact, densely branched habit, but bears slightly larger semi-double flowers with carmine-red sepals surrounding a white, red-veined corolla, blooming heavily from early summer through fall. Its small stature suits rock gardens, path edges, and the front of a hardy fuchsia border, and it draws hummingbirds despite its diminutive size. It dies back to the ground in colder winters and resprouts reliably from the roots each spring. In the humid, hot summers of the Gulf South it performs best with afternoon shade and consistent soil moisture, and a heavy winter mulch over the crown helps it return at the cooler edge of its hardiness range.

common_name: Jack Shahan Fuchsia (Large Single Pink Trailing Fuchsia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants after frost danger has passed in rich, well-drained, evenly moist potting mix in shade to partial shade; an American-bred trailing fuchsia prized for its unusually large single pink flowers on a vigorous basket plant.

directions: Grow in a hanging basket or shaded container filled with rich, well-drained, evenly moist potting mix. Jack Shahan bears exceptionally large single flowers in soft rose-pink throughout, without the sharp color contrast typical of many fuchsias, on long trailing stems that make it one of the most popular pink basket cultivars among American Fuchsia Society growers. Its vigorous, self-branching habit fills a basket quickly and flowers heavily from late spring through fall in favorable conditions. It has little cold tolerance and, like most trailing fuchsias, dries out quickly as a basket plant, so in the Gulf South site it in a shaded, breezy spot with frequent watering and bring it under cover well before the first fall frost.

common_name: Army Nurse Fuchsia (Upright Violet-and-Red Hardy Fuchsia)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; a vigorous, exceptionally cold-tolerant hardy fuchsia long grown in American gardens for its reliable winter survival.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Army Nurse bears semi-double flowers with deep red sepals surrounding a violet-blue corolla that ages to reddish purple, held in abundance on a sturdy, upright, well-branched bush from early summer through fall. It is among the most reliably cold-hardy of the upright hardy fuchsia cultivars, regularly returning from the roots even after harsh winters that kill less hardy selections. In the humid, hot summers of the Gulf South it still benefits from afternoon shade and consistent soil moisture, since fuchsias in general dislike prolonged high heat, but its vigor makes it more forgiving than many cultivars. Mulch the roots heavily going into winter to protect the crown, especially at the colder edge of its range.

common_name: Rose of Castile Fuchsia (Historic White-and-Purple Hardy Fuchsia)

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in early summer or plant container-grown plants in moist, fertile, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; a Victorian-era hardy fuchsia introduced in England in 1855 and still grown for its refined, softly colored flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Rose of Castile bears white sepals faintly flushed pink surrounding a violet-purple corolla that ages toward magenta, a softer, more refined color combination than the bold red-and-purple typical of hardy fuchsias, blooming from early summer through fall on an upright, well-branched bush. Introduced in the mid-1800s, it remains one of the oldest hardy fuchsia cultivars still in general cultivation and draws hummingbirds reliably throughout its long bloom season. It dies back to the ground in colder winters and resprouts from the roots each spring. In the humid, hot summers of the Gulf South it performs best with afternoon shade and consistent soil moisture, and a heavy winter mulch over the crown improves its odds of returning at the cooler edge of its hardiness range.
